messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Blank line following \end{knitrout}
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can remove the blank line after \end{knitrout}, but even you
do that, the following text is still a separate paragraph in default
knitr LaTeX output. Here is how to do it (set the 'document' hook to
replace '\end{knitrout}\n'):

\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

Knitr replaces \texttt{@} with an empty string so that it becomes a
blank line in the tex output.

<<setup>>=
knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  gsub('(\\\\end\\{knitrout\\})\n', '\\1', x)
})
@

See if it works.
<<>>=
# hello world
1+1
@
This line should continue as a part of the above paragraph instead of
a separate paragraph.

\end{document}

This is due to the kframe environment (anything after it becomes a new
paragraph). If you want the Sweave style, you can simply use
render_sweave() (it will set all the options you mentioned). But at
the moment, there is a tiny problem that I need to solve (will do it
soon).

That said, an alternative way to solve this problem is to add
\noindent automatically, e.g.

knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  gsub('(\\\\end\\{knitrout\\}[\n]+)', '\\1\\\\noindent ', x)
})

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: eval=FALSE and prompt problem
messages.body_plain:
It appears that when I use an eval=FALSE directive in a chunk, that each line after the first line is considered to be a “continuation” of the first.  Thus, if I use traditional R prompts in the chunk, each line after the first is preceded with a “+” rather than a “>”.  Code for a minimal example is shown below, with the resultant PDF attached (see second or ‘problem-spot’ chunk).  Thank you in advance for any help with this “problem.”

\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

<<setup, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE>>=

opts_chunk$set(prompt=TRUE)

@

You can test if \textbf{knitr} works with this minimal demo. OK, let's get started with some boring random numbers:

<<boring-random>>=

set.seed(1121)

x <- rnorm(20)

mean(x)

var(x)

@

<<problem-spot, eval=FALSE>>=

mean(x)

var(x)

@

<<>>=

sessionInfo()

@

\end{document}

In theory you can write any languages in knitr besides R. There are
some which are already supported like Python, Ruby, Awk, Bash, ... I
have a series of hello world examples under
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/

For example,

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/027-engine-bash.Rmd
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/027-engine-bash.md

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/023-engine-python.Rmd
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/023-engine-python.md

For your stumbling blocks:

1. You can customize how markdown is converted to HTML in RStudio, but
I do not really like the way of customization:
http://www.rstudio.org/docs/authoring/markdown_custom_rendering

I will probably talk to them later, but anyway, you can define your
own converter to ignore the base64 encoding step.

2. Again, you can define a custom converter to do that. Markdown to
PDF is not a natural conversion, although Pandoc has done a lot of
work. HTML lives best in the web browser, and PDF is best for
printing. For example, you do not need to worry about pages in the web
browser (because everything is in one continuous page), but that is a
big challenge when you do typesetting in PDF.

I understand people tend to be greedy (write one and generate all),
but there is just no free lunch :) We have to make a decision on which
output format is primary and which is secondary.

Regards,
Yihui

Old versions of RStudio may have problems with finding add-on
packages. The first thing that you can do is to make sure you are
using the latest version of RStudio. If the latest version does not
work, check

find.package(c('ggplot2', 'rdatamarket'))

In your case, I bet rdatamarket was installed in a different library
location. Reinstall this package may help. If the problem still
exists, you need to report to
